newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-A LOVE-LY LOOK AT WINGED FOOT.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-A LOVE-LY LOOK AT WINGED FOOT.

text.p: Davis Love's second round in the PGA Championship, a roller-coaster one-over-par 71 after a record-tying 66, could be considered a textbook example of golf at famed Winged Foot Golf Club.

"This course is going to get you if you miss one shot," the 33-year-old son of a famous teaching pro -- and one of the best golfers yet to win a major championship -- said after making four birdies, three bogeys and a double bogey in a round that included just about everything that Winged Foot offers.

The famous course designed by A.W. Tillinghast didn't wait long to get Love, who bogeyed the first hole, a 446-yarder that played as the most difficult in the first round of the PGA Championship, which is the fifth major that the club as hosted.

After a good drive, Love had 175 yards to the hole, but his 6-iron came up a bit short. He chipped onto the green, but just not quite far enough -- and the ball rolled backwards almost off the putting surface. Love two-putted for bogey.
Two holes later, Love hit a 3-iron on the 216-yard par-3 that drifted into a big bunker on the right side of the green -- a feature on almost every hole at Winged Foot.
He blasted out of the deep sand pit but only reached the fringe of the green. A chip and a putt gave him another bogey.
Love, however, used his famous length to get those two strokes back on the fifth and sixth holes -- perhaps two of Winged Foot's easiest, especially for a long hitter.
"You have to hit two good shots on every hole to have a chance for birdie -- and that's not easy," Love said later.
But he made it look easy on the 515-yard, par-5 fifth, where he hit a driver and 3-iron to 10 feet and two-putted for birdie.
Sticking to the two-good-shots game plan, he also birded the 324-yard sixth hole, where he hit 3-iron and sand wedge to 18 feet and drained the putt.

However, a poor drive at the 442-yard eighth, which ended up in the trees lining the left side of the fairway, led to another bogey. While Love somehow managed to hit a 9-iron over the trees to the green, he couldn't get it close to the hole and wound up three-putting.

Love, who said that Winged foot's two par-5s (there are four for the members) are the only real birdie opportunities, took full advantage of what little the 6,987-yard, par-70 course offerd by also making birdie at the 540-yard 12th.
He also birdied the 423-yard 15th, hitting a 1-iron and an 8-iron to within four feet.
But then disaster struck at the dificult 457-yard 16th, where Love drove with a 3-wood into deep rough and tried to hit a 1-iron 225 yards to the green.
"That 1-iron wasn't very smart," he said later. His ball again would up in trees and his only shot was to pitch it into a greenside bunker and hope for a good up-and-down.
It didn't happen. Love blasted onto the green, but not close enough to sink the putt, leaving him with his only double bogey of the championship.
"I feel I can recover from bad shots. I just don't need to make bad decisions," Love said, referring to his decision to hit a 1-iron out of Winnged Foot's extremely thick rough.
"I was trying to make an easy par and I made an easy double bogey," he added ruefully.
Love also said there is another feature of Winged Foot that can punish a player -- its slippery, sloping greens, where Love had several lipped-out putts.
"You can't cut them much faster, or else seven over par will win," he said.
A good example was the 18th hole, where Love's 30-foot birdie try spun out of the hole. "It dove down in and then came out," Love said of the putt.
Still, despite his adventures, Love, who led the field by a stroke before his double bogey at 16, was neither disappointed nor discouraged.
"After two days, being (three) under par on this golf course I feel I have a chance to win," he said.
That is, if Winged Foot does not get any more difficult, as Love well knows.
"They can go crazy here where you couldn't break 80," Love said. One could almost see him shudder as he said it.
